extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, students, and teachers seeking information on The Elements of Style and writing/style guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and extract the guidance and evaluative criteria that The Elements of Style (Strunk & White) presents for clear American English prose, including its enumerated rules, principles, matters of form, and stylistic reminders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary rules of usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A compact set of eight 'elementary rules of usage' presented by Strunk (1918) and retained in later editions; these are concrete rules governing grammar and word usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia article notes these eight rules collectively and gives examples drawn from them: exhortations such as 'omit needless words,' 'use the active voice,' and 'employ parallelism appropriately.' These rules are aimed at producing clean, correct usage in American English prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary principles of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of ten 'elementary principles of composition' that guide how to construct sentences and paragraphs for clarity and force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principles emphasize clarity, economy, and arrangement of material. The book's teachings (expanded by White) are summarized as advocating 'cleanliness, accuracy, and brevity in the use of English' and include the oft-quoted injunctions about concision and vigorous writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: A few matters of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, practical rules about matters of form: punctuation, formatting, and small conventions of written presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article mentions that later editions include matters of form (e.g., punctuation practice such as contemporary recommendations for punctuating names). These are practical, low-level style choices intended to standardize presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and expressions commonly misused
rubrics_metrics.description: A compiled list (49 items in some editions) of words and expressions that writers commonly use incorrectly or imprecisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section includes prescriptive corrections and replacement suggestions. The Wikipedia article cites one example area ('They. He or She') where the book advises modern alternatives to the generic masculine and flags usages that can convey unintended emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words often misspelled
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of frequently misspelled words (57 items in some editions) intended as a reference to improve accuracy in spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a practical reference list for writers to consult to avoid common orthographic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reminders for better style
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of 21 brief 'reminders' (in later editions) that encapsulate recurring stylistic advice for clearer, better prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These short reminders are distilled aphorisms (the last being 'Prefer the standard to the offbeat') meant to shape a writer's habitual choices toward conventional, lucid expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to style / writer mindset
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice about the writer's attitude and approach: write to please yourself and seek 'one moment of felicity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White's concluding chapter 'An Approach to Style' recommends a mindset—favoring clarity, personal satisfaction in writing, and striving for moments of felicitous phrasing—rather than purely mechanical rule-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words (conciseness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The explicit injunction to 'omit needless words'—i.e., to be concise so every word 'make[s] every word tell.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted passage (Strunk, 1918): 'Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences...' Guidance stresses that concision does not mean all sentences must be short or that detail should be eliminated, but that unnecessary words should be removed so prose is tight and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to prefer active-voice constructions over passive ones where appropriate, to produce more direct, vigorous prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of Strunk's core usage recommendations to increase clarity and force; critics have debated the borderline cases, but the book's position is a general preference for active constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ parallelism appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise ensuring parallel grammatical structure in coordinated elements (parallelism) to improve clarity and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among Strunk's elementary exhortations; parallelism is presented as a tool for clarity and balance in sentence construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the standard to the offbeat
rubrics_metrics.description: A stylistic maxim (the final of the 21 reminders): favor standard, conventional expressions over deliberately offbeat or quirky choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reminder encapsulates the book's conservative stylistic stance: conventional phrasing is usually clearer and preferable to unusual constructions that may distract or confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generic masculine pronouns; use inclusive alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A later-edition recommendation to avoid using 'he' as a generic pronoun and to use 'they,' 'he or she,' 'you,' or 'the writer' instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fourth edition replaces earlier generic-masculine advice with guidance acknowledging gendered-language concerns and suggesting inclusive alternatives to avoid unintentional emphasis on the masculine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid split infinitives (prescriptive prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, Strunk & White discouraged split infinitives; the Wikipedia article reports critics noting this prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book's proscription of split infinitives is cited by critics (e.g., Pullum) as an example of overly prescriptive advice; the article records the existence of the rule in Strunk & White rather than defending it as linguistically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict 'which' to non-restrictive clauses (prescriptive guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strunk & White have been read as advising that 'which' should not be used in restrictive relative clauses (i.e., prefer 'that' for restrictive uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia entry notes critics' objections that the book proscribes otherwise established usages (such as the use of 'which' in restrictive clauses), again highlighting a prescriptive stance that some linguists consider mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness, accuracy, and brevity (overall goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching aims promoted by the book: writing that is clean (clear and well-ordered), accurate (precise in meaning and usage), and brief (concise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White described Strunk's manual as 'a forty-three-page summation of the case for cleanliness, accuracy, and brevity in the use of English.' These three terms function as high-level evaluative criteria for good prose according to the work.
